name: Censorship of poetry, drama, and music
plain_explanation: Plato bans large parts of Homer and Hesiod, forbids most drama, and restricts which musical modes and rhythms children may hear, all in order to shape virtuous, courageous, and obedient citizens from an early age.
precise_definition: A state-controlled censorship regime covering literature ('music' in the broad sense) presented to the young, justified on the grounds that stories depicting misbehaving gods, expressions of fear of death, excessive laughter, or indulgence in feasting and lust would corrupt future guardians, and that dramatic imitation of villains, women, or inferiors would degrade actors and audiences of good birth.
why_it_mattered: It shows the illiberal cost, in Russell's reading, of subordinating culture entirely to a predetermined civic and military purpose, and it directly inspired later real-world censorship regimes invoking similar justifications.
historical_origin: Modeled partly on actual Spartan restriction of harmonies to the Dorian and Phrygian modes.
examples: Only the Dorian (courage) and Phrygian (temperance) musical modes are allowed; the Lydian (sorrow) and Ionian (relaxation) are banned.
All dramatists are to be ceremonially honored and then banished from the city, since a good man should not imitate villains, women, or inferiors.
objections: Russell notes the impossibility Plato himself half-recognizes: plays without any flawed characters are not really possible, which is precisely why Plato ends up banishing dramatists altogether rather than reforming drama.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Plato insists the young be taught that 'evils never come from the gods,' reshaping traditional religious stories to serve civic education.
